newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters "confused" over coalition deals, says Clark.
newsitem.headline: Peters "confused" over coalition deals, says Clark.

text.p: Aspects of the so-called "secret" coalition deal revealed last week by New Zealand First leader Winston Peters had been agreed with Labour but not with National, according to Labour leader Helen Clark.
Peters had become confused between the two offers, the New Zealand Press Association reported her saying.
Peters on Friday revealed what he claimed were agreements with National that had been negotiated too late to be included in the written coalition agreement.
They included:
* more money for the Commissioner for Children
* government funding of a class action on behalf of victims of nuclear testing at Christmas Island
* an investigation into investment advice given by the BNZ in the 1980s
* the establishment of an anti-corruption commission
* a referendum on republicanism
* an investigation into lump-sum compensation for victims of the "bad blood scandal" who picked up hepatitis C or HIV from contaminated blood supplies.
The revelations, which took government officials by surprise, were dubbed a "secret deal" by Labour deputy leader Michael Cullen.
On Sunday Prime Minister Jim Bolger said while the issues had been discussed during the last day of coalition talks they had not been agreed.
There would be no BNZ inquiry and there was no agreement for a referendum on republicanism, though if republicanism became a live issue in future it would have to be put to a referendum.
"There were a number of issues that came up right at the concluding stages of the negotiations. We did not seek to resolve them in detail."
Many of the issues would be resolved, but he did not anticipate them being part of any formal coalition agreement.
He dismissed NZ First leader Winston Peters' reference to the issues as an "addendum" to the coalition agreement, saying: "I would describe them as points that were raised."
Clark told NZPA Labour had agreed to deal with the BNZ, bad blood and Christmas Island issues, as well as the establishment of an anti-corruption commission.
It had not committed to a referendum on republicanism in the current Parliamentary term, but had said that if republicanism became a live issue in future it would have to be put to a referendum.
All of the issues had been dealt with before Tuesday, when NZ First negotiators raised them with National.
"They are all things that we had understandings of but they weren't agreed to (with National)...I think he (Mr Peters) has got confused."
A spokeswoman for Bolger said the government was working through the bad blood and Christmas Island issues and would announce details later of what had been resolved.
The issues had not been agreed during coalition talks, so could not be referred to as a "secret deal".
Peters' press secretary Mike Booker, said he did not accept Peters was confusing the two sets of talks.
"I don't think so. They (the issues) were certainly raised with National. The Prime Minister acknowledged that."
